body.stem: A junior administrator is uncertain which scope level they selected on an assignment they just saved. They show you the four strings below, each taken from a different assignment in different subscriptions. Which string represents a resource group scope?

options.text: /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/corp-mg
/subscriptions/aaaa1111-bb22-cc33-dd44-555555eeeeee
/subscriptions/aaaa1111-bb22-cc33-dd44-555555eeeeee/resourceGroups/sales-rg
/subscriptions/aaaa1111-bb22-cc33-dd44-555555eeeeee/resourceGroups/sales-rg/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/customerdata

explanation.correct: A resource group scope ends at /resourceGroups/{resourceGroupName} and has no further /providers path. The correct option matches that pattern and is therefore a resource group scope.

perChoice.a: This string has the /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/ prefix, which is the format used for a management group scope.
perChoice.b: This string ends at /subscriptions/{subscriptionId} with no further path, which is the format used for a subscription scope.
perChoice.d: This string continues past /resourceGroups/{name} into /providers/.../storageAccounts/{name}, which is the format used for a resource scope (specifically a storage account), not a resource group scope.

body.stem: A single subscription contains a resource group named sales-rg that holds many resources, including exactly one storage account containing the blob data the team needs to read. You want to give a small read-only team the Storage Blob Data Reader role so they can read blobs in that one specific storage account, and you want the assignment to grant them no other access anywhere in sales-rg, the subscription, or any other resource group in the same subscription. At which scope should you create the role assignment?

exhibit.text:
Hierarchy:
  Subscription
    └── sales-rg  (resource group)
          ├── storage account (the one with blob data)
          ├── other resources
          └── ...

Other resource groups in the subscription:
  hr-rg, finance-rg, dev-rg

Management group above the subscription:
  corp-mg

options.text: The storage account
The sales-rg resource group that contains that storage account
The subscription that contains that storage account
A management group containing the subscription that holds the storage account

explanation.correct: The storage account resource scope is the narrowest level and grants access only to that specific resource. Any scope broader than the resource itself would grant permissions to additional resources in the same group, subscription, or beyond.

perChoice.b: Assigning at the resource group scope grants access to every resource inside sales-rg, including other resources that share that group with the storage account, exceeding the stated least-privilege goal.
perChoice.c: Assigning at the subscription scope grants access to every resource in the subscription, including all other resource groups, exceeding the stated least-privilege goal.
perChoice.d: Assigning at the management group scope grants access across every subscription under that management group, exceeding the stated least-privilege goal.

body.stem: You run a PowerShell command to inspect a role assignment and review only the Scope property in the output shown. At which scope level is the assignment applied?

exhibit.text:
Scope              : /subscriptions/aaaa1111-bb22-cc33-dd44-555555eeeeee/resourceGroups/sales-rg/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/customerdata
DisplayName        : Finance Readers
RoleDefinitionName : Storage Blob Data Reader
PrincipalType      : Group

options.text: management group
subscription
resource group
resource

explanation.correct: The Scope value continues past the /resourceGroups/{name} segment into a /providers/.../storageAccounts/{name} segment for a specific storage account, which is the format of a resource scope rather than a resource group scope.

perChoice.a: A management group scope has the format /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/{managementGroupName}, which this Scope value does not start with.
perChoice.b: A subscription scope ends at /subscriptions/{subscriptionId}, with no further /resourceGroups segment, which this Scope value does include.
perChoice.c: A resource group scope ends at /resourceGroups/{resourceGroupName}, with no further /providers segment, but this Scope value continues into /providers/Microsoft.Storage/...

body.stem: A junior administrator reports that the current assignment counts in the exhibit are accurate. They have a request from engineering to add 80 more role assignments directly at the sub-billing subscription scope, granting 80 new engineer accounts read access to that subscription's resources. All 80 requested assignments will be active (permanent). What must the administrator do to satisfy the request?

exhibit.text:
Scope                                  Current active role assignments
Subscription      sub-billing            4,950
Management group  corp-mg                480

Documented limits:
  - Up to 5,000 role assignments per subscription (includes assignments at the subscription, resource group, and resource scopes)
  - Up to 500 role assignments per management group
  - Eligible and future-scheduled assignments do not count toward these limits

options.text: Add 80 more assignments at the sub-billing subscription scope; the resulting total of 5,030 stays below the 5,000 maximum because eligible and time-bound assignments are exempt from the count.
Add the 80 assignments at the sub-billing subscription scope; the new total of 5,030 fits inside the 5,000 maximum because only assignments at the resource scope count, not at the subscription scope.
Reject the request because adding 80 more assignments would push the total past the maximum for a single subscription.
Reject the request because the corp-mg management group already has 480 assignments and would reach its 500-assignment maximum as soon as those new assignments are added.

explanation.correct: The documented limit is 5,000 role assignments per subscription, and that limit counts active assignments at the subscription, resource group, and resource scopes. Adding 80 more active assignments at the sub-billing subscription scope would bring the total above 5,000, so the request must be rejected.

perChoice.a: Eligible and time-bound (future-scheduled) assignments are exempt from the count, but the 80 requested assignments are active and therefore do count, so 5,030 is not within the limit.
perChoice.b: The per-subscription limit explicitly includes role assignments at the resource group and resource scopes as well, so an assignment at the subscription scope is not the only kind counted.
perChoice.d: The 80 new assignments are added at the sub-billing subscription scope, not at the management group scope, so they do not count toward the corp-mg management group limit.

body.stem: You manage a subscription that contains exactly three resource groups: web-rg, api-rg, and data-rg. The assignments shown in the table are the only ones that exist for this identity. The web team reports that the identity can still create and delete web apps in web-rg, but their policy allows only list and read actions there. Full management rights are still required in api-rg and data-rg. Which change should you make?

options.text: Remove the subscription-level Contributor assignment and create new Contributor assignments at api-rg and at data-rg, keeping the read-only assignment at web-rg
Keep the subscription-level Contributor assignment and add another Reader assignment at web-rg, so the narrower scope governs that resource group
Change the subscription-level Contributor assignment to point at api-rg, then create a second Contributor assignment for data-rg
Create a deny assignment at the subscription scope that blocks this identity from deleting resources anywhere in the subscription

explanation.correct: Azure RBAC is additive: the effective permissions of a principal are the sum of every role assignment that applies to it, and the scope hierarchy is parent-child, so the subscription-level assignment still contributes all of its actions for resources inside web-rg. Narrowing access therefore means taking the broad assignment away and recreating the permissions only where they are still needed. Deleting the subscription-level Contributor assignment and creating new Contributor assignments at api-rg and data-rg leaves web-rg governed solely by its read-only assignment.

perChoice.b: Adding another read-only assignment at web-rg cannot subtract anything: the subscription-level Contributor assignment still applies inside web-rg and its actions remain part of the effective permissions, so the identity keeps full management rights there.
perChoice.c: The scope of a role assignment is fixed when the assignment is created; it isn't repointed in place. To move the rights you would have to delete the subscription-level assignment and create new ones, which is what the keyed option does.
perChoice.d: A deny assignment blocks the listed action for every resource in its scope. Created at the subscription scope it would also block deletes in api-rg and data-rg, where full management is required, and it would leave the identity's other write rights inside web-rg intact.

body.stem: Your security team must be able to manage access in every subscription that sits anywhere under the corp management group, and the platform team keeps adding new subscriptions there. Which scope should you choose for their role assignment?

options.text: The scope of the corp management group
The scope of each subscription directly under corp, created one by one
The scope of the platform management group
The scope of a resource group named corp in each subscription

explanation.correct: Management groups sit above subscriptions in the hierarchy and can themselves nest, so an assignment made at corp is the single broadest place to cover both child management groups and the subscriptions beneath them. Because lower levels inherit permissions from higher levels, anything later placed under corp — including new subscriptions — is covered without further assignments.

perChoice.b: Assigning at each subscription would have to be repeated every time a subscription is added, which conflicts with the stated goal, and it ignores the nesting of the management groups.
perChoice.c: The platform management group covers only the subscriptions beneath platform; the analytics branch and its subscription would be left unmanaged.
perChoice.d: A resource group is a narrower level below a subscription, so an assignment made there reaches only resources in that group, not the subscriptions and other resource groups of the subscription.

body.stem: You deploy the template below with the resource group deployment command against pay-rg, which already holds other storage accounts. The readers on the finance team must be able to read blob data in stpayprod001 and must reach none of the other accounts in pay-rg. How should you change the template?

options.text: Add a scope setting to the role assignment resource so that it applies only to stpayprod001
Nest the role assignment resource inside the stpayprod001 resource block in the template
Rename the role assignment resource to the resource ID of stpayprod001
Put the role assignment resource in a separate template file and deploy that file against stpayprod001

explanation.correct: Without a scope on the role assignment, the assignment inherits the level of the deployment, so a resource group deployment produces an assignment covering everything in pay-rg. When the assignment has to sit at the level of an individual resource, the role assignment must carry the scope that points at that resource, so setting it to stpayprod001 limits the readers to that single account and leaves the rest of pay-rg untouched.

perChoice.b: The documented way to assign a role at the level of a resource is to set the scope property on the role assignment. Moving the block inside the storage account does not replace it, and the assignment still takes its level from the deployment.
perChoice.c: The name identifies the assignment itself. Role assignment names are typically a GUID, and a name that looks like a resource ID does not redirect where the assignment applies.
perChoice.d: Deployments target a tenant, management group, subscription, or resource group, never an individual resource. A second template deployed to that resource group produces another assignment at the same broad level.

body.stem: You administer a tenant whose hierarchy is listed in the exhibit. Five teams each need one role assignment, and the security policy forbids giving anyone reach beyond what the team actually needs. Drag each team's requirement to the scope value you should use for its assignment.

rows: Management group that contains SUB-A, SUB-C and MG-2
Management group inside MG-1 that contains SUB-B

items.text: The audit team must read everything under the top grouping, including anything placed there later.
The Europe operations team must manage everything under the grouping that holds only SUB-B, including subscriptions added to it later.
The database team must manage everything in SUB-B and reach nothing outside it.
The finance operations team must manage everything in R4 and reach nothing beyond it.
The reporting team must list the files in CT-6 and reach nothing else.

slots.label: /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/corp-mg
/providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/eu-mg
/subscriptions/11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111/resourceGroups/ledger-grp
/subscriptions/11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111/resourceGroups/ledger-grp/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stledger01/blobServices/default/containers/invoices

explanation.correct: Each team receives the narrowest scope that still covers its full requirement. The audit team's reach spans every subscription anywhere beneath the top grouping, present and future, so it goes at MG-1. The Europe operations team's requirement is deliberately about the nesting group that currently holds only SUB-B and must also cover subscriptions placed there later, so it goes at MG-2 rather than at the subscription itself. The database team is confined to one subscription, the finance operations team to one resource group inside a subscription, and the reporting team to a single container inside a storage account, giving three different and increasingly specific scope formats.

perChoice.i1: Assigning at MG-1 reaches every subscription under that grouping, and because the assignment stays attached to the grouping, subscriptions added beneath it later are covered too. A subscription or resource group scope would miss the sibling subscriptions.
perChoice.i2: The requirement is about the grouping that sits above SUB-B and about subscriptions that will be added to it later, so the grant belongs at MG-2. The subscription scope would cover today's SUB-B but would not pick up future subscriptions placed in the grouping.
perChoice.i3: The team needs everything inside one subscription and nothing outside it, which is the subscription scope built from the subscription ID alone. A resource group scope would be too narrow and a management group scope would be too broad.
perChoice.i4: The requirement covers one resource group within a subscription, so the scope is the subscription ID followed by the group name. A subscription scope would hand the team every other group, and a single resource scope could not cover future resources created in the group.
perChoice.i5: The requirement names one container inside one storage account, so the scope is the full resource path down to the container. Any shorter scope would expose the rest of the storage account, the group or the subscription.

body.stem: You administer one grouping, two subscriptions and their workloads, all listed in the exhibit. Your team creates access grants by deploying templates, and each template carries a role assignment resource whose name you choose. Drag each team's requirement to the name that role assignment resource must carry so the grant reaches exactly what the team needs and nothing more.

rows: Management group that contains SUB-9 and SUB-5

items.text: The security team must be able to manage access across the top grouping, and across anything placed beneath it in future.
The product team must manage anything created in SUB-9, whatever resource group it is created in.
The platform operations team must manage what is in R3 and nothing outside it.
The reporting team must manage only A7 and reach nothing else in R3.

slots.label: /providers/Microsoft.Management/managementGroups/tenant-core/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/ra-7712
/subscriptions/44444444-4444-4444-4444-444444444444/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/ra-7712
/subscriptions/44444444-4444-4444-4444-444444444444/resourceGroups/prod-grp/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/ra-7712
/subscriptions/44444444-4444-4444-4444-444444444444/resourceGroups/prod-grp/providers/Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/stapp01/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/ra-7712

explanation.correct: A role assignment always hangs off the object whose access it changes: its name is the name of that object followed by the authorization provider segment and the assignment ID, so the coverage of the grant is the path of the extended object. The security team's grant is extended by the grouping itself, the product team's by the subscription, the platform operations team's by the resource group, and the reporting team's by the single storage account.

perChoice.i1: Coverage must include every subscription under the grouping, now and in future, so the role assignment is created against the grouping and its name starts with the management group path. Extending the subscription would leave the sibling subscription and anything added later uncovered.
perChoice.i2: Coverage is everything created in one subscription regardless of where inside it the resources land, so the role assignment is created against the subscription and its name starts with the subscription ID. Extending a resource group would miss resources created in other groups of that subscription.
perChoice.i3: Coverage is one resource group and nothing else, so the role assignment is created against that group and its name carries the subscription ID followed by the group name. Extending the subscription would be too broad; extending the storage account inside it would be too narrow.
perChoice.i4: Coverage is limited to one storage account, so the role assignment is created against that account and its name carries the full provider path for the account before the authorization segment. Extending the group would expose every other workload in it.

body.stem: You have the grants in the exhibit and no others anywhere in the tenant. You need to confirm what each group can actually reach today. Drag each group to the description of what its access covers.

rows: tenant-core, the management group above sub-prod and sub-emea
rg-app, a resource group inside sub-emea
vnet-sales, a virtual network inside rg-app
No assignment recorded for this group

items.text: sec-ops
db-team
app-team
net-team
audit-team

slots.label: Everything inside one subscription and nothing outside it
Nothing at all, because no grant exists for this group
One virtual network and nothing around it
Everything beneath the grouping, including subscriptions added to it later
Everything inside one resource group only

explanation.correct: Permissions granted at one level flow down into everything nested beneath it and stop at the edges of that object. An assignment on the management group therefore reaches every subscription under it, present and future; an assignment on the subscription reaches all of its groups and resources but nothing in the sibling subscription; an assignment on the resource group stops at that group's boundary; an assignment on a single resource reaches only that resource. A group with no assignment reaches nothing.

perChoice.g1: Its grant sits on the management group, so it covers everything beneath that grouping, and because the assignment is attached to the grouping, subscriptions placed under it later fall inside its reach as well.
perChoice.g2: Its grant sits on sub-emea, so it reaches every group and resource in that subscription and stops there; the sibling subscription is outside the reach.
perChoice.g3: Its grant sits on one resource group inside sub-emea, so it reaches that group's workloads and nothing in the other groups of the same subscription.
perChoice.g4: Its grant sits on one virtual network, the most specific kind of target, so it reaches that network alone and not the surrounding group.
perChoice.g5: No assignment is recorded for this group, and permissions only come from role assignments, so it reaches nothing at all.

body.stem: Before the operations team creates its next round of grants, colleagues need the exact value to hand to the tooling as the scope. For some targets only a friendly name is on file. Drag each situation to the way of producing that value.

rows: ledger-grp, a resource group in the subscription with ID 66666666-6666-6666-6666-666666666666
Subscription ID and the group name
archive, a blob container inside the storage account streports01
A grant already exists for this account

items.text: The platform team holds the GUID of the subscription and the name of the group that carries its workloads.
The finance team has only the friendly name of one blob container.
A colleague created a grant through the portal for one storage account, and the exact stored value is needed.

slots.label: Written out by hand from what the admin knows
Copied from the object's property sheet
Read back from the record itself

explanation.correct: Coarse targets are easy to build by hand because their identifiers are predictable: a resource group value is the subscription ID followed by the group name, and a subscription value is the ID on its own. A single nested resource such as a blob container has a much longer path, so it is taken from the resource's own identifier in the portal, and an existing assignment can always be listed to read back the exact value that was stored with it.

perChoice.i1: For a resource group the value is built from facts already held: the subscription ID plus the group name. No lookup is needed, which is why this one is written out by hand.
perChoice.i2: A container sits several levels below the subscription, so its path cannot be guessed from a friendly name alone. Opening the container in the portal and reading the identifier shown in its properties gives the exact value.
perChoice.i3: When a grant already exists, listing the role assignments with command-line tooling and reading the coverage value reported for that assignment returns precisely what was stored, with no guesswork.

body.stem: Alice was granted the Reader role at the scope of one virtual machine that lives in a resource group named 'hr-rg'. She has no other role assignments anywhere in the tenant. She is curious about how this grant applies to a second virtual machine that also lives in the same resource group 'hr-rg'. What is Alice's effective access to the second virtual machine?

exhibit.text:
PS /> Get-AzRoleAssignment -SignInName alice@contoso.com -Scope "/subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourceGroups/hr-rg/providers/Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/payroll-vm"

RoleAssignmentId   : /subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourceGroups/hr-rg/providers/Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/payroll-vm/providers/Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/aaaa1111-bbbb-2222-cccc-3333dddd4444
Scope              : /subscriptions/00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000/resourceGroups/hr-rg/providers/Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/payroll-vm
DisplayName        : Alice Park
SignInName         : alice@contoso.com
RoleDefinitionName : Reader
ObjectId           : 55555555-6666-7777-8888-999999999999
ObjectType         : User

options.text: She has full access because both resources live in the same resource group and resource-scope role assignments automatically extend to peer resources.
She has Reader access because Reader role assignments always extend to every resource in the parent container regardless of the original scope.
She has Reader access only to the targeted virtual machine because role assignments at the resource scope do not extend to peer resources in the same resource group.
She has no access to any virtual machine because the Reader role cannot be assigned at the resource scope and only works at subscription or resource-group scope.

explanation.correct: This is the correct option because role assignments apply strictly to the scope at which they are created. A role assignment at the resource scope covers that one specific resource only; it does not extend laterally to peer resources that share the same parent container. Each peer resource needs its own separate role assignment before the principal can act on it.

perChoice.a: This option is incorrect because role assignments do not propagate laterally between peer resources. Inheritance in Azure RBAC flows downward through the scope hierarchy (parent to child), so a grant at one resource does not reach the other resources in the same resource group.
perChoice.b: This option is incorrect because the scope of a role assignment determines exactly what it covers; it does not automatically widen to every other resource in the parent container. Only an assignment written at the parent scope, such as the resource group itself, would reach every resource inside it.
perChoice.d: This option is incorrect because Reader is a built-in role that can be assigned at any of the four scope levels: management group, subscription, resource group, or individual resource. Azure RBAC places no restriction on using Reader at the resource scope.

body.stem: Your tenant has a Microsoft Entra ID P2 license, so the assignment type options are offered at the scopes where they are supported. Three access requests are waiting in the queue. Drag each request to the assignment type that satisfies it.

rows: Members of the Release-Engineering group (Microsoft Entra ID users)
Every resource group in subscription sub-finance
A duty manager must approve every request, and the permission should lapse on its own afterwards
Members of the Audit-Team group (Microsoft Entra ID users)
Access is needed only for the evidence window that opens on 1 March and closes on 31 May; the team neither requests nor approves anything
System-assigned managed identity of function app payfunc001
Every storage account in resource group reports-rg, including accounts added later
It has to keep working continuously without anyone taking part

items.text: R1 — release engineers need Contributor in sub-finance
R2 — auditors need Reader in sub-archive
R3 — the payfunc001 identity needs Storage Blob Data Reader in reports-rg

slots.label: Eligible assignment
Active assignment, time bound duration
Active assignment, permanent duration

explanation.correct: The Assignment type tab appears for management group, subscription, and resource group scopes, and both assignment types exist there; which one fits depends on whether the principal must activate the role and how long the permissions last. R1 asks for an approval step and automatic expiry, which only the eligible type provides. R2 asks for permissions limited to fixed start and end dates with no activation step, which is an active assignment with a time bound duration. R3 asks a managed identity for continuous access, and managed identities can never receive the eligible type because they cannot perform activation steps, so it takes an active assignment with permanent duration.

perChoice.i1: R1 requires a duty manager approval before the role can be used and requires the permission to lapse automatically afterwards. The eligible assignment type does exactly this: the user must perform one or more actions, such as providing a business justification or requesting approval, and Privileged Identity Management settings govern the lifetime of the assignment. The target is a subscription, one of the scopes where the options are offered.
perChoice.i2: R2 needs permissions that begin on a chosen date and end on another one, with no request or approval involved. That is an active assignment whose duration is set to time bound, with the start and end date and time supplied. Choosing permanent duration would leave the auditors with read access after the evidence window closed.
perChoice.i3: R3 is a system-assigned managed identity, and eligible assignments cannot be created for applications, service principals, or managed identities because they cannot complete the activation steps, so an active assignment is the only option. The request also asks for continuous access with no end date, which matches the permanent duration setting. The resource group reports-rg is a scope where the options are offered, and the inheritance from the resource group scope covers storage accounts added later.

body.stem: The three role assignments in the exhibit are the only ones that exist in this tenant, and every person mentioned below belongs only to the groups named for them. Support has written up the four outcomes that surprised the teams involved. Match each outcome to the behavior of Azure RBAC that produces it.

items.text: Permissions granted at a broad scope are inherited by every resource and group underneath it
Permissions from several grants are summed, so an extra assignment at a smaller scope cannot remove anything
Membership is transitive: being inside one group that is inside another carries the enclosing group's permissions
Access stops as soon as the role assignment that supplied it is deleted at that scope

slots.label: Kim, who sits in Group Platform, updates a virtual machine under the corp grouping even though no entry names that machine
Priya sits in both Group Finance-Ops and Group Finance-Readers; adding the second left her with exactly what the first already provided
Lee is listed only on Group Prod-Deployers, yet reaches the same resources as Group Platform
Group Platform members can no longer do anything anywhere in the tenant, and nothing of theirs is listed at the corp grouping anymore

explanation.correct: Azure RBAC combines four effects that the four reports are each showing: permissions flow down the parent-child scope hierarchy, permissions from several assignments are added together rather than cancelled out, group membership is transitive, and access exists only for as long as the assignment that grants it. Each outcome therefore maps to exactly one of those behaviors, decided by what the exhibit and the report state.

perChoice.i1: Kim reaches the virtual machine through G1, the Owner assignment created at the management group scope, even though that entry names only the grouping. Roles can be assigned at any of the four scope levels, and lower levels inherit the permissions from higher levels, so everything beneath a subscription inside that management group is covered. This is why nothing in the exhibit has to name the machine.
perChoice.i2: Priya holds Contributor from G2 at the subscription and Reader from G3 at the finance-rg inside that same subscription. Azure RBAC is an additive model in which effective permissions are the sum of the role assignments, so the Reader permissions add nothing new to what Contributor already allowed and subtract nothing either. A smaller-scope assignment can never reduce the broader one.
perChoice.i3: Lee has no direct entry of her own; she is only inside Group Prod-Deployers, which is itself inside Group Platform. Role assignments are transitive for groups, so membership in the outer group gives her the permissions that group holds through G1, even though she was never added to Group Platform directly.
perChoice.i4: The loss of reach for Group Platform follows from how access is granted and taken away: a principal gains access through the creation of a role assignment and loses it when that assignment is removed. Deleting G1 at the management group scope ended the permissions for every subscription and resource group beneath it, which is why members report that they can do nothing anywhere and that nothing of theirs shows up at that grouping.

body.stem: Your tenant has a Microsoft Entra ID P2 license. The service desk team must be able to request elevation for a limited period, with their manager's approval, but only for the virtual machines that run in prod-app-rg. When you open the Add role assignment page for a single virtual machine, the options that would let you mark the grant as eligible or time bound are not shown. Which scope should the service desk assignment be created at?
body.statement: The service desk assignment should be created at {{scope}}.

options.text: the resource group that holds the virtual machines
the subscription that holds the resource group
the individual virtual machine resource
the management group that holds the subscription

explanation.correct: The assignment type choices - eligible, or active with a permanent or time-bound duration - are only offered for management group, subscription, and resource group scopes. Because the service desk must reach nothing beyond the virtual machines in prod-app-rg, the resource group is the only scope that both offers those choices and keeps the grant inside the stated requirement.

perChoice.scope:a: The resource group scope is listed among the scopes where the assignment type and duration options are offered, and prod-app-rg limits the grant to the virtual machines the service desk actually supports.
perChoice.scope:b: The subscription scope also offers the eligible and time-bound options, but an assignment there would let the service desk activate the role over every resource in the subscription, including those outside prod-app-rg.
perChoice.scope:c: At the scope of a single resource such as one virtual machine, the portal does not offer the assignment type or duration options, which is exactly why they were missing on the page you opened.
perChoice.scope:d: A management group assignment does offer those options, but it would reach every subscription placed under that management group, well beyond what the service desk team needs.

body.stem: A junior administrator follows the documented steps for granting Azure access. On the Access control (IAM) page, the Role assignments tab works, but the Add role assignment command is greyed out and nothing happens when it is clicked. The security team checks which actions the junior administrator's group is authorized for. Which action must that group hold before the command becomes available?

rows: Role assignments tab opened at the level of pay-rg
Lists the assignments created for pay-rg
Option greyed out, page never opens
Action audit for the junior administrator's group

body.statement: Before that command can be used, the group has to be authorized for {{action}}.

options.text: Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write
Microsoft.Authorization/policyAssignments/write
Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write
Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/write

explanation.correct: Creating a role assignment is itself an authorized operation, so the person doing it needs Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write at the scope where the assignment is created, or at a higher scope. Built-in roles such as Role Based Access Control Administrator and User Access Administrator include this action. Without it the portal greys out the Add role assignment option, which is the behaviour described here.

perChoice.action:b: That action covers creating policy assignments, not role assignments. It grants nothing over who can be given which role, so the Add role assignment option stays unavailable.
perChoice.action:c: This action manages virtual machines. It says nothing about creating role assignments, which is the operation the junior administrator is trying to perform.
perChoice.action:d: This action manages storage accounts. Like the virtual machine action, it belongs to the resource provider of a service and does not enable role assignment creation.

body.stem: The storage account stpay001 holds the payroll data the auditors must read. An ARM read-only lock is in place on that account, and every attempt to create their assignment against the account itself, or against a container inside it, fails with an authorization error. The auditors need read-only reach into blob data, with no ability to change or delete anything. Which scope should their assignment be created at?
body.statement: The auditors' assignment should be created at {{scope}}.

options.text: the resource group pay-rg
the storage account stpay001
the blob container named exports
the subscription that owns pay-rg

explanation.correct: When a storage account carries an Azure Resource Manager read-only lock, the lock blocks role assignments that are scoped to the storage account or to a container within it. Creating the assignment one level higher, at pay-rg, is therefore the way to get the grant in place, and choosing a data-reader role definition keeps the reach limited to reading blob data rather than any management rights.

perChoice.scope:a: The read-only lock only blocks assignments scoped to the storage account or a container, so an assignment at the level of pay-rg is created successfully, and a data-reader role definition keeps it read-only.
perChoice.scope:b: This is one of the two scopes the read-only lock blocks, which is why attempt 1 returned AuthorizationFailed. An assignment scoped to the account cannot be created while the lock is in place.
perChoice.scope:c: A container inside the account is the other blocked scope, as attempt 2 shows. Scoping the assignment to a single container fails for the same reason as the account-level attempt.
perChoice.scope:d: A subscription-scoped assignment would be created without hitting the lock, but it would hand the auditors reach over blob data in every storage account in the subscription, which is wider than they need.

body.stem: Late last night your automation ran az role assignment create so the audit group could read blob data in the storage accounts underneath it, and the command finished without errors. This morning the auditors still receive authorization errors when they list a container in those accounts. What is the right explanation to give them?
body.statement: The explanation to give the auditors is that {{cause}}.

options.text: a grant created at a management group scope can take much longer to become effective than one created at a narrower scope, so the auditors should keep retrying
a grant created at a management group scope becomes effective within the same short window as every other grant, so the command must have targeted the wrong scope
a grant created at a management group scope never reaches the data inside an object, so a separate data access role must be added at each subscription
a grant created at a management group scope is honoured only by the management plane, so the auditors have to create it from the portal instead

explanation.correct: Creating or removing role assignments can take up to ten minutes to take effect, and the documentation warns that an assignment created at the management group scope can take much longer. Both commands finished cleanly and the assignment created against pay-rg already works, so the remaining denial is the propagation delay, not a mistake in the scope value.

perChoice.cause:b: The short window applies to assignments at narrower scopes. Treating a management group assignment as already effective sends you hunting for a wrong scope value when the real cause is propagation time.
perChoice.cause:c: Nothing in the documentation says a data access role created at the management group scope fails to reach data; it only notes that such an assignment takes longer to propagate. Adding roles at each subscription is not the remedy.
perChoice.cause:d: The command line tool is the documented way to create a data access role, including at narrow scopes such as a container, and the same propagation behaviour applies whatever tool is used. Switching to the portal does not speed anything up.

body.stem: The data team holds the Contributor role on the ml-rg resource group, and that is the only assignment any of its members has across the whole tenant. Tomorrow a new virtual machine is deployed to ml-rg. What happens to the data team's access to that new virtual machine?

rows: Any other assignment for this principal

options.text: They can work with it the same way they already work with everything else inside that resource group
They get no access to it, because a grant reaches only the resources that already existed when it was created
They can read it but not change it, because anything created later arrives without any access
They can act on it only after a fresh assignment is created for that resource group

explanation.correct: Scopes sit in a parent-child relationship and lower levels inherit the permissions granted at higher levels, so the Contributor assignment created on ml-rg flows down to everything contained in ml-rg. A virtual machine deployed there afterwards is covered by the existing assignment exactly like the resources already there.

perChoice.reach:b: This is the opposite of how scopes behave. Permissions granted on a resource group flow down to the resources inside it, so something deployed there later is covered rather than excluded, and the assignment does not freeze at the moment it was created.
perChoice.reach:c: Nothing inside ml-rg is read-only by default. The single Contributor assignment already carries full management permissions over everything in that resource group, including the new virtual machine.
perChoice.reach:d: No second assignment is required. The permissions are already granted on ml-rg, and the contents of ml-rg inherit them, so nothing has to be recreated when the new virtual machine appears.

body.stem: You administer access for Contoso's operations team, whose remit covers exactly the two resource groups marked as needed in the exhibit. The security policy states that the team must reach nothing else in the tenant, and those two resource groups sit in different subscriptions. You may add as many grants as the change process allows. Which approach should you take?

rows: Management group containing sub-billing and sub-inventory

body.statement: To satisfy the policy, you should {{grantPlan}}.

options.text: assign the Contributor role at the scope of each listed resource group
assign the Contributor role at the scope of each listed subscription
assign the Contributor role at the scope of the management group above both subscriptions
assign the Contributor role at the scope of a single listed resource group

explanation.correct: A role assignment takes effect at exactly the scope where it is created, and a resource group is a valid scope on its own. Creating one Contributor assignment at the scope of pay-rg and another at the scope of inv-rg gives the team management rights over the contents of both areas and nothing outside them, because every wider scope in the exhibit (the two subscriptions and the management group above them) also contains targets the policy excludes.

perChoice.grantPlan:b: The exhibit shows platform-rg inside sub-billing and warehouse-rg inside sub-inventory. An assignment created at subscription scope reaches every resource in that subscription, so it would hand the team management rights over areas marked as no access.
perChoice.grantPlan:c: A management group is a scope above subscriptions, and an assignment there applies throughout every subscription beneath it, which is wider than the two resource groups the team owns.
perChoice.grantPlan:d: An assignment applies only at the scope it was created at, so covering just one of the two resource groups leaves the team's other area unreachable.
